DPI explained — pick the right one for your use case

DPI (dots per inch) controls the resolution of the output images. Higher DPI = larger image dimensions = bigger file size = sharper output. Here's what each option actually produces and when to use it:

96 DPI is screen resolution — the same density your monitor displays. A typical A4 PDF page at 96 DPI becomes roughly a 794×1123 pixel image. File sizes are small (50–150 KB per page for a typical document). Use this when you just need to share a page on WhatsApp, post it somewhere online, or quickly preview content. Text is readable at normal screen size but looks soft if you zoom in.

150 DPI is the sweet spot for most people. An A4 page becomes about 1240×1754 pixels — large enough to read all text clearly, small enough that the ZIP doesn't become unwieldy. Use this for sharing presentations slide-by-slide, extracting charts from reports, or turning a PDF brochure into image assets. This is the default because it covers 90% of real use cases well.

200 DPI produces A4 images around 1654×2339 pixels. Text remains sharp even at moderate zoom. Use this when the PDF contains small print, fine diagrams, or tables with tight columns that would look blurry at 150 DPI. Also good if you're inserting the images into a presentation or document where they'll be displayed at a reasonable size.

300 DPI is print resolution. An A4 page becomes 2480×3508 pixels — the standard for professional printing. Each image will be 500 KB to several MB depending on content. Use this only if you're sending images to a printer, creating high-quality print assets, or need pixel-perfect clarity for small text and fine details. For screen use, 300 DPI is overkill and just makes the ZIP file large.

PNG vs JPG — which format to choose

The right choice depends on what's in your PDF, not just on file size preference.

Use PNG when your PDF contains text, diagrams, charts, tables, screenshots, or any content with sharp edges and flat colours. PNG is lossless — every pixel is preserved exactly. Text stays crisp, lines stay clean, and there are no JPEG compression artifacts around high-contrast edges. PNG files are larger than JPG, but for document content the quality difference is clearly visible, especially at 96–150 DPI.

Use JPG when your PDF consists mainly of photographs or scanned images with natural tones and gradients. JPG compression is designed for photographic content — it removes detail that human eyes don't notice in photos, producing much smaller files with minimal visible quality loss. At quality 92 (what this tool uses), JPG output looks very close to the original photo. The trade-off: text and line art in JPG output often shows subtle blurring and artifacts around edges, which becomes obvious at 100% zoom.

A common mistake: using JPG for a text-heavy PDF to save space, then finding the text looks slightly blurry and the output file is barely smaller than PNG would have been. For mixed-content PDFs (some text, some photos), PNG is the safer choice.

What this tool actually does under the hood

This tool uses PDF.js — Mozilla's open-source PDF renderer, the same engine that powers Firefox's built-in PDF viewer — to render each page of your PDF to an HTML canvas element at the resolution you selected. It then exports each canvas as a PNG or JPG image and packages all images into a ZIP file using JSZip. Everything happens inside your browser tab. Your PDF is loaded into memory, rendered locally, and never sent anywhere.

One thing worth knowing: PDF.js renders PDFs as they would appear on screen, which means the output images accurately reflect how the document looks visually. However, if your PDF contains vector graphics or text, they get rasterized (converted to pixels) in this process. The output images are not editable — they're flat pixel images of what the pages look like.

Common use cases

Sharing individual pages: WhatsApp, Telegram, and most messaging apps display images inline but show PDFs as file attachments that people have to tap to open. Converting PDF pages to images makes content immediately visible in the conversation without extra taps. Use 150 DPI JPG for small file sizes that load quickly on mobile.

Extracting charts and diagrams: If a report or presentation contains charts you want to reuse in another document, converting to images is the fastest way to extract them. Use 200 DPI PNG to preserve the chart quality for use in slides or documents.

Posting document content online: Social media platforms (LinkedIn, Twitter/X, Instagram) accept images but not PDFs. Converting a certificate, infographic, or report page to an image lets you post it directly. Use 150–200 DPI JPG for social media — it keeps file sizes small enough for fast uploads.

Creating thumbnails or previews: If you need a preview image of a PDF's cover page for a website or portfolio, 96 DPI JPG produces a clean, lightweight thumbnail.

Frequently asked questions

Why is my output image blurry even at 300 DPI?

This usually means the source PDF itself has low-resolution content. If the PDF was created from scanned images that were scanned at 150 DPI, rendering the PDF at 300 DPI won't recover detail that wasn't there to begin with — the PDF.js renderer scales up what it has, which produces a larger but not sharper image. The DPI setting controls the output canvas resolution, not the quality of the source content. If your source images were low resolution, the output will be too.

Can I convert just one page instead of all pages?

Not directly in this tool — it converts all pages and packages them in a ZIP. If you only need one page, use the PDF Split tool first to extract that single page as its own PDF, then convert just that one-page PDF here. You'll get a ZIP containing a single image.

My PDF has 50 pages. Will this still work?

Yes, though it will take a while — each page needs to be rendered individually, and higher DPI means more pixels to process per page. At 150 DPI, a 50-page A4 document typically takes 30–90 seconds depending on your device's CPU speed. At 300 DPI, expect 2–4 minutes. The progress bar tracks page-by-page so you can see it working. Keep the browser tab active during conversion — some browsers throttle background tabs.

Does the output preserve the PDF's colours accurately?

Yes, for standard RGB-colour PDFs. PDF.js renders colours accurately for typical documents. The exception is PDFs with CMYK colour profiles (common in professionally printed materials) — PDF.js converts CMYK to RGB for rendering, which can cause subtle colour shifts. For colour-critical work (print design, brand materials), use Adobe Acrobat for PDF-to-image conversion instead.

HEIC images won't load — why?

This is about the Images to PDF tool, but worth mentioning here: HEIC is Apple's proprietary image format and browsers don't natively support it. Convert HEIC to JPG first (iOS Photos app → Share → Save as JPG, or use an online HEIC converter), then use that JPG here. This tool only accepts PDFs as input, so HEIC isn't directly relevant, but it's a common point of confusion when going the other direction.
